title: The laugh that connects
text: Laughter is thirty times more likely in company than alone, which tells you it is not really about jokes. It is a {{1}} — the only human signal that requires the whole respiratory system, impossible to fake convincingly and {{2}} contagious that hearing it on a recording can set a room {{3}}. Neuroscience {{4}} the social story: laughter in company activates the brain's mirror regions, {{5}} in empathy, and couples who laugh together report closer bonds years later. The content, meanwhile, barely matters. Most conversational laughter follows {{6}} remarks — 'see you later', 'I know' — punctuation for warmth rather than responses to wit. That is why laughter {{7}} in every culture yet sounds identical everywhere, and why fake laughter is detectable: genuine laughs are faster, higher and less controlled. Chimpanzees laugh when chased — the play {{8}} of a baby being tickled — which suggests the behaviour is at least thirty million years older than comedy. We did not invent laughing. We inherited it.

gaps.explanation: 'it is a broadcast' — a signal sent to an audience; bulwark = a defensive barrier.
'so contagious that…' — 'so + adjective + that' is the fixed pattern; 'very contagious that' is ungrammatical.
'set a room off' — trigger it, like an alarm; 'set up' means arrange, 'set out' means display.
'neuroscience backs the social story' — supports it; ban = forbid.
'regions involved in empathy' — taking part in it; invoice = bill someone.
'follows mundane remarks' — ordinary everyday phrases; morbid = grimly concerned with death.
'laughter occurs in every culture' — takes place; incur = bring a cost upon oneself, concur = agree.
'the play squeal of a baby being tickled' — the excited high-pitched cry; squint = look with half-closed eyes.
